summaries.summary: The paper motivates keyword-based autocomplete, noting left-to-right systems can be inefficient and exploring tradeoffs among typing efficiency, reconstruction accuracy, and keyword interpretability.
Supervised keyword-sentence datasets are expensive and static, while unsupervised joint learning can produce communication schemes uninterpretable to humans.
The proposed unsupervised autocomplete system restricts keywords to source-sentence subsequences and uses multi-objective optimization to control efficiency-accuracy tradeoffs.
Naively optimizing a linear combination is unstable, so the authors optimize communication efficiency under an accuracy constraint, improving stability and efficiency at all accuracy levels.
The framework yields schemes 52.16% more accurate than rule-based baselines at 77.37% of sentences, 11.73% more accurate than weighted optimization at 53.38%, and saves nearly 50% of time.
A communication game has a user pass keywords z from target sequence x using q_{\alpha }(z\mid x), while the system guesses x via p_{\beta }(x\mid z).
A good communication scheme (q_{\alpha }, p_{\beta }) uses fewer keywords as cost and reconstructs target sentence x with high probability as loss.
Schemes are restricted to potentially noncontiguous subsequences of the target sentence to ensure interpretability by retaining important content words.
An encoder models q_{\alpha }(z\mid x) by retaining token subsets, with Bernoulli sampling over token-retention probabilities to keep or drop tokens independently.
The decoder p_{\beta }(x\mid z) conditions on keywords z and predicts x using a standard sequence-to-sequence model with attention and copying.

The goal is to learn encoder-decoder pairs balancing communication cost and reconstruction loss, with the simplest approach weighting \mathrm {cost}(x, \alpha ) and \mathrm {loss}(x, \alpha , \beta ) linearly using \lambda.
Naively weighting and searching over \lambda is suboptimal and unstable, as slight changes produce degenerate schemes keeping all or none of the tokens.
The main technical contribution frames the tradeoff as constrained optimization problems minimizing expected cost subject to varying expected reconstruction error constraints \epsilon.
The constrained objective improves training stability, gradually drops uninformative words, and lets \epsilon directly control maximum reconstruction error unlike \lambda.
To optimize the constrained objective, the authors consider the Lagrangian of Eq (DISPLAY_FORM6).
Unbiased gradients use minibatch averages, and although convergence is guaranteed only for convex objectives, optimization is stable and outperforms Eq (DISPLAY_FORM5).
Optimization with respect to q_{\alpha }(z\mid x) is difficult because z is discrete, so the authors use the stochastic REINFORCE estimate BIBREF5.

Joint updates on (\alpha , \beta , \lambda ) use standard gradients for \beta and \lambda, and an unbiased stochastic gradient estimate for \alpha with one sample and a moving-average reward baseline.
The approach trains on 500K randomly sampled Yelp reviews sentences, measuring efficiency by token retention rate and accuracy by exact matches from greedy decoding.
Figure FIGREF10 shows the constrained objective yields more efficient schemes than the linear objective at every accuracy level, including 11.73% more accuracy at 53.38% retention rate.
The linear objective is unstable with \lambda, degenerating at \lambda \le 4.2 and \lambda \ge 4.4, while the constrained objective is substantially more stable with \epsilon.
The efficiency-accuracy tradeoff is compared with Unif and Stopword baselines, whose decoders are optimized by gradient descent to minimize \mathrm {loss}(x, \alpha , \beta ).
Figure FIGREF10 shows similar baseline tradeoff curves, while the constrained model achieves 52.16% accuracy improvement at 77.37% retention rate compared to Unif.
Additional robustness results and analysis of correlations between token retention rates and token properties are deferred to the Appendix.
The user study recruited 100 Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) crowdworkers across 50 sentences, comparing autocomplete keyword tasks with writing tasks and top three suggestion judgments.

Table TABREF13 shows under-specified keywords yield generic suggestions, over-specified keywords yield almost identical sentences, and properly specified keywords are completed with added words and punctuation.
The top suggestion was semantically equivalent 80.6% of the time, one of the top 3 was equivalent 90.11%, exact match was 18.39%, and keyword typing took 3.86 seconds versus 5.76 seconds.
The authors thank reviewers and Yunseok Jang, and acknowledge support from NSF CAREER Award IIS-1552635 and an Intuit Research Award.
All code, data and experiments are available on CodaLab at https://bit.ly/353fbyn.
